Welcome to Echo Basin National Park

Where the mountains answer back

Echo Basin is 186,000 acres of glacier lake, old-growth cedar and high country, about two and a half hours from the city. We're open all year. Most people come for the lake. Almost everybody ends up yelling at the mountains from Echo Point, because they yell back.

Four landscapes, one park

The park climbs more than 5,000 feet in eleven miles, so you can paddle the lake in the morning and be standing in snow by lunch. Here's what you pass on the way up.

  1. 8,560 ft

    Echo Pass

    Snow most of the year, and a warming hut that's staffed all summer. The view from the top is the one on the postcards. On the way up, stop at Echo Point and give it a yell. Four echoes is normal.

  2. 6,230 ft

    Halloran Meadows

    Wildflowers peak in July. Elk graze here most evenings, so bring binoculars and keep your distance. It's also the only spot in the park where you can see the lake and the pass at the same time.

  3. 4,270 ft

    Cathedral Stand

    Old-growth cedar and Douglas fir, some of it more than 600 years old. The boardwalk loop is flat and wheelchair accessible. Please stay on it, because the roots are shallower than they look.

  4. 3,540 ft

    Echo Lake

    Eleven miles long and cold enough to make you yelp. On calm mornings it's a mirror. Canoes and kayaks rent by the hour at the lodge dock, life jackets included.

Day hikes

Five maintained trails, from a flat stroll along the lake to a full day in the snow. Mileage is round trip. Grab a paper map at either entrance station, because your phone won't work past the lodge.

How the echo works

Shout from the rail at Echo Point and you'll hear it four more times. Four cliffs on the slope below Halloran Meadows face the point, the nearest about 600 feet off and the farthest more than half a mile, and sound only travels about 1,100 feet a second. The last echo takes five and a half seconds to get back. June does a short echo talk up there at 10 and 2, and she brings a stopwatch.

Meet the rangers

We have 31 rangers in summer and about a dozen through the winter. These four run most of the public programs, so chances are you'll meet at least one of them.

  • Ines Okafor

    Chief Ranger

    Nineteen seasons at Echo Basin. Runs the 7 am canoe tour on Saturdays and will absolutely race you back to the dock.

  • Tomás Reyes

    Backcountry Ranger

    Patrols Echo Pass on skis from November to May and keeps the Pass Hut stocked. Makes the best camp coffee in the park, according to him.

  • June Halvorsen

    Interpretive Ranger

    Gives the Echo Point talk at 10 and 2. Can name every bird in the basin by ear and will quiz you on them.

  • Sam Whitlow

    Trail Crew Lead

    Rebuilt the Cathedral Stand boardwalk over three summers. Ask him about cedar if you have an hour to kill.

Wildlife

More than 200 species live in the park. Please give all of them room: 25 yards for elk and deer, 100 yards for bears. If an animal changes what it's doing because of you, you're too close.

Roosevelt elk
A herd of about sixty grazes Halloran Meadows at dawn and dusk. The bulls bugle through September and you can hear it from the lodge.
Common loon
Two pairs nest on Echo Lake. Listen for them around dusk.
Great horned owl
Lives in Cathedral Stand year round. You can often hear one from the lodge porch after dark.
Black bear
Around forty in the park. Every campsite has a bear locker. Please use it, and yes, that includes toothpaste.
Seen something we missed?
Tell us at any ranger station. Good sightings go in the park log with your name on them.

Today in the park

The pass usually runs about 20 degrees colder than the lake, so check both temperatures before you pick a trail, and check sunset before you pick a long one. Tracks are easiest to find first thing in the morning, in the mud along the Lakeshore Loop.

Updated every morning by 6 at the lodge front desk and both entrance stations.

Know before you go

  1. Carry water

    A liter for every two hours of hiking, more in July. Lake and stream water has to be filtered.

  2. Stay on the trail

    Shortcuts kill meadow plants that take twenty years to grow back. Also, we find lost people a lot faster when they stayed on a trail.

  3. Lock up your food

    Use the bear locker at your site. Coolers and tents don't count.

  4. Make noise on blind corners

    Bears would rather hear you coming. Talk, clap, sing badly.

  5. Check conditions

    Weather at the pass can turn in an hour. Call the ranger line or stop at a station before you head up.

  6. Sign the trail register

    Sign in at the trailhead and sign out when you're back. If you don't sign out, we come looking.

ECHO BASIN PARK AUTHORITY. Internal, do not post.

To: all district staff
From: I. Okafor
Date: Sept. 13
Re: dusk procedure (replaces yesterday’s)

  1. Everybody indoors by dusk. That includes search teams. I know.
  2. No names on the radio, post numbers only. It's picked up eleven names so far and it uses them.
  3. When you talk to visitors or pose for photos, keep your back to the trees. It comes closer when somebody is looking at it.
  4. Log the bark and crown damage as wind. Log the height as forty feet. It's taller than that. Sam thinks it crouches to get under the canopy.
  5. If a visitor reports a fifth echo, get them inside and don't tell them the fifth one was their own voice.
  6. Knock at door height and say the room number. Guests have been told anything else isn't us.

Lodging and camping

Basin Lodge has 24 rooms and six cabins on the water. Cedar Flats has 80 campsites back in the trees. Summer weekends sell out by March, so book early or come midweek.

  • Lodge room

    from $189/night

    Includes breakfast and an hour of canoe rental. Half the rooms face the lake, so ask for one of those.

  • Lakeside cabin

    from $240/night

    Sleeps four. Wood stove, kitchenette, and about twenty steps to the dock.

  • Cedar Flats campsite

    $28/night

    Fire ring, picnic table, bear locker, and a water tap every few sites. Quiet hours are 10 pm to 6 am.

  • Backcountry permit

    $12 per group

    Required for overnight trips above Halloran Meadows. Pick it up in person at the ranger station.

Dark sky programs

The nearest town is sixty miles away, so the sky here gets properly dark. On a clear night at the pass you can see the Milky Way without even trying. Rangers set up telescopes outside the Pass Hut on Friday and Saturday nights from June through September. It's free and you don't need to book.

  • Star talks: Fri and Sat, 9 pm, outside Pass Hut
  • Dress warm and bring a red flashlight
  • Moonrise tonight: 9:14 pm

Plan your visit

Passes are $30 per vehicle and good for seven days. Buy one at either entrance station, or online before you come. The road to the lodge is plowed all winter.
